findings.title: Denial cache key does not include the identity type
findings.body: The denial key is built only from namespace, the raw subject UID, action, resource name, and parent folder, but permission resolution switches on identity type and returns different permission sets for the same UID. In particular, anonymous and render-service subjects both use UID "0", while anonymous receives Viewer-role permissions and the render service is granted read access to all dashboards and folders. A denial recorded for anonymous:0 can therefore short-circuit and incorrectly deny render:0 for the same dashboard for up to the denial TTL, and the same collision can occur between user and service-account spellings. The key must include the identity type, preferably together with the canonical resolved UID.

findings.title: Denial cache key concatenation is ambiguous
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins variable-length UID, action, name, and parent values with plain underscores and no escaping, length prefixes, or hashing. Distinct tuples can consequently produce the same key: for example name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the same suffix. Grafana resource and folder UIDs may contain underscores, so a denial for one resource can incorrectly deny a different resource until the entry expires. Build the key from a structured, unambiguously encoded or hashed tuple.

findings.title: Denial entries shadow fresher permissions and undermine immediate access after a grant
findings.body: Check consults permDenialCache before checking the ordinary permission cache, and neither getUserPermissions' permission-cache refresh nor List's refresh deletes existing denial entries. After a permission is granted, such as the creator permission inserted for a new dashboard or folder, a later check or list for another resource can refresh permCache with a scope map that now allows the denied resource, yet checks for that resource will still return the old denial until the denial TTL expires. A denial recorded by a check made just before the grant has the same effect. This partially defeats the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created resources immediately; cached allowances should be honoured before denials or denials should be invalidated when permissions are refreshed.

findings.title: Every distinct cached denial now forces a database permission fetch
findings.body: When cached permissions do not allow a check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and the permission-store cache lookup was removed from getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so this performs a fresh database permission query. The new denial cache only suppresses repeats for the exact namespace/user/action/name/parent tuple for 30 seconds. A user checking many distinct dashboards or folders they do not own therefore causes one permission query per resource instead of one query per user/action as before, multiplying database load in denial-heavy or enumeration-heavy workloads and increasing cache cardinality. The revalidation needs a freshness or negative-cache strategy that does not scale database queries with the number of distinct denied resources.

findings.title: Denial-cache test would pass even if the denial cache were ignored
findings.body: The test named "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" sets the permission cache to map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}; despite the comment saying this allows access, checkPermission treats a false map value as no permission, and the fake permission store also returns no granting permission. The request therefore denies through the ordinary cached/DB path even if permDenialCache is never consulted, so the test does not prove the new short-circuit works. It should configure the underlying store or permission cache to allow dash1, or assert that the permission store is not called when the denial entry is present.
